content: Respiratory failure or respiratory distress is the most common reason for unplanned hospital admissions and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions in infants. Non-invasive respiratory support methods are now preferred over invasive techniques like intubation and mechanical ventilation, as they are associated with fewer complications. High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is increasingly being used as a non-invasive respiratory support method. However, there is limited evidence regarding its use in term infants (defined as infants born at or after 37 weeks of gestation and up to one month of age), and there is no consensus on its safety and efficacy in this population. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of HFNC oxygen therapy for respiratory support in term infants compared to other non-invasive respiratory support methods. A systematic search of multiple databases, including Cochrane CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and others, was conducted in December 2022. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving term infants (≥ 37 weeks gestational age) up to one month of age were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Meta-analyses were performed when studies were sufficiently similar, and the GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. Eight studies involving 654 participants were included in the review. Six studies (625 participants) contributed data to the primary analyses. Four studies compared HFNC oxygen therapy with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for respiratory support in term infants. In two studies (439 infants), the outcome of death was reported, but no deaths occurred in either group. HFNC may have little to no effect on treatment failure, but the evidence is highly uncertain (risk ratio [RR] 0.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47 to 2.04; 3 trials, 452 infants; very low-certainty evidence). Chronic lung disease, defined as the need for supplemental oxygen at 28 days of life, was reported in one study (375 participants), but no cases were observed in either group. HFNC may have little to no effect on the duration of respiratory support (mean difference [MD] 0.17 days, 95% CI -0.28 to 0.61; 4 trials, 530 infants; very low-certainty evidence). HFNC likely results in little to no difference in the length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU) (MD 0.90 days, 95% CI -0.31 to 2.12; 3 trials, 452 infants; moderate-certainty evidence). HFNC may reduce the incidence of nasal trauma (RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.66; 1 trial, 78 infants; very low-certainty evidence) and abdominal overdistension (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.71; 1 trial, 78 infants; very low-certainty evidence), but the evidence is very uncertain. Two studies compared HFNC with low-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy (LFNC), defined as supplemental oxygen delivered at a maximum flow rate of 2 L/min. The outcome of death was reported in both studies (95 infants), but no deaths occurred in either group. HFNC may slightly reduce treatment failure (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.92; 2 trials, 95 infants; low-certainty evidence). Neither study reported data on chronic lung disease. HFNC may have little to no effect on the duration of respiratory support (MD -0.07 days, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.69; 1 trial, 74 infants; very low-certainty evidence), length of stay in the ICU (MD 0.49 days, 95% CI -0.83 to 1.81; 1 trial, 74 infants; very low-certainty evidence), or overall hospital length of stay (MD -0.60 days, 95% CI -2.07 to 0.86; 2 trials, 95 infants; very low-certainty evidence), but the evidence is very uncertain. Adverse events were reported in both studies (95 infants), but no adverse events occurred in either group. The risk of bias across outcomes was generally low, although some concerns of bias were noted. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, with downgrades due to risk of bias, imprecision, indirectness, and inconsistency. In conclusion, when compared with CPAP, HFNC may result in little to no difference in treatment failure. HFNC may have little to no effect on the duration of respiratory support, but the evidence is very uncertain. HFNC likely results in little to no difference in the length of stay in the ICU. HFNC may reduce the incidence of nasal trauma and abdominal overdistension, but the evidence is very uncertain. When compared with LFNC, HFNC may slightly reduce treatment failure. HFNC may have little to no effect on the duration of respiratory support, length of stay in the ICU, or overall hospital length of stay, but the evidence is very uncertain. There is insufficient evidence to develop evidence-based guidelines for the use of HFNC in term infants. Larger, well-designed trials are needed to better understand the potential benefits and risks of HFNC in this population.
